source: Lenat and Brown (1983/1984) Why AM and Eurisko Appear to Work
finding: AM was an automatic programming system. A math concept was a small Lisp predicate. New concepts came from small syntactic mutations of that code, steered by empirical findings and heuristics. The authors say much of AM's success came from the density of worthwhile math concepts when written as Lisp, not from the heuristics alone.
numbers: Worked example, June 1976 run: LIST-EQUAL returned T on about 2% of random list pairs (about 50 example lists). That rarity triggered 'generalize', which gave three new predicates L-E-1 (same length), L-E-2 (same first element), L-E-3. From same-length AM derived length, then natural numbers, addition and elementary number theory.
quote: it was only because of the intimate relationship between Lisp and Mathematics that the mutation operators turned out to yield a high hit rate
limits: Retrospective self-critique by the AM author. No hit-rate count is given. The text we read is OCR and noisy.
agent_relevance: Proposal quality depends on the representation. Small edits to a well-matched representation are mostly viable. If our lemma or subgoal format is too fine-grained, edits give garbage. Keep lemmas short and in the problem's own vocabulary.

source: Lenat and Brown (1983/1984) Why AM and Eurisko Appear to Work
finding: The same mutation scheme failed when pointed at heuristics. Mutating two-page Lisp heuristics almost always gave useless or worse-than-useless rules. Eurisko only improved after heuristics were rewritten as many small slots, so one slot edit macro-expands into many coordinated code edits. AM's ultimate limit was its inability to find new domain-specific heuristics.
numbers: Five years of mediocre results on heuristic discovery before the representation change; heuristic bodies shrank often by an order of magnitude. Eurisko split a slot into sub-slots in three cases (one in 3D VLSI design).
quote: such point mutations are almost universally deleterious
limits: Qualitative. No ablation counts.
agent_relevance: Conjecturing works where the conjecture space is dense with true, useful items (math concepts). It fails where it is sparse. Do not expect free-form invention of new strategies or operators to work. Use fixed templates.

source: Ritchie and Hanna (1984) AM: a case study in AI methodology
finding: Methodological critique of AM. The published descriptions do not match the program's behaviour in places, and the techniques behind its impressive output are obscure. Argues for rational reconstruction instead of large impressive programs with unstated theory.
numbers: No experiment. Artificial Intelligence 23(3), pp 249-268.
limits: Seen only as abstract and search summary this session.
agent_relevance: Claims of discovery by a loop need an audit of what was built in by hand. Our own lemma loop should log what was seeded.

source: Colton, Bundy and Walsh (1999) Automated Discovery in Pure Mathematics (HR project note)
finding: HR represents a concept as a data table and has 10 production rules that turn old concepts into new ones. It spots a conjecture when a new concept's table equals an old one. It sends conjectures to the prover Otter and to the model finder Mace for counterexamples, which are added to the data. It scores interestingness by parsimony, complexity, discrimination, proof difficulty and surprisingness.
numbers: Best result: refactorable numbers (the number of divisors divides the number). The concept was missing from the OEIS and was added. HR conjectured they are 0, 1, 2 or 4 mod 8, later proved; also all odd refactorables are squares.
limits: Short project note. Few counts of how many conjectures were junk. Results are for number theory and algebra.
agent_relevance: A conjecture loop gets stronger with a counterexample channel: refuted conjectures become data for later conjectures. Equal outputs between two constructions is a cheap conjecture trigger.

source: Claessen, Smallbone and Hughes (2010) QuickSpec: Guessing Formal Specifications using Testing
finding: QuickSpec generates terms from a function signature, tests them on random data, groups terms into equivalence classes, reads equations off the classes, then prunes equations that follow from earlier ones with congruence closure. Without pruning the output is far too long.
numbers: Raw step gives 5,000 to 50,000 equations. The target is tens. After pruning the heap library case study gives a short complete set. Adding list operations to the signature found toList (fromList xs) == sort xs, i.e. heapsort.
quote: the number of equations should be in the tens, not hundreds or thousands
limits: Testing is unsound: some equations may be false. Quality depends on test generators. Only equations. Case studies are Haskell heaps and an Erlang fixed-point library, no hit-rate table.
agent_relevance: Most of the work in conjecturing is filtering. Test cheaply first, then prune what is implied by what you already hold. Richer vocabulary (adding related functions) gave the best laws.

source: Johansson and Smallbone (2021) Conjectures, Tests and Proofs: An Overview of Theory Exploration
finding: Overview of QuickSpec and its use as a lemma discovery front end. Conjecture generators fall in three families: heuristic rule-based (AM, HR, MATHsAiD), term generation plus testing (QuickSpec, Graffiti, IsaCoSy, IsaScheme, Speculate) and neural. QuickSpec's only interestingness test is that a term is not reducible by what is known.
numbers: Vampire on 50 TIP inductive benchmarks: 7 proved alone; plus 18 more with QuickSpec conjectures as lemmas (90-line script), 25 total (3 problems timed out in QuickSpec). HipSpec proved 44, CLAM 41 (partly interactive), Zeno 21 on the same set. QuickSpec scales to about 30 functions or term size about 9.
quote: Graffiti's set of examples was fixed, leading to production of relatively many non-theorems
limits: Survey by the tool authors. Comparison across systems used different setups.
agent_relevance: Lemma discovery nearly quadrupled the number solved by a general prover (7 to 25 of 50). The main cost is search space growth, so keep the signature small and relevant to the goal.

source: Johansson and Smallbone (2021) Conjectures, Tests and Proofs: An Overview of Theory Exploration
finding: Compares neural conjecturers with testing-based ones. Neural conjecturers produce duplicates of the library and non-theorems. QuickSpec rarely produces false or duplicate conjectures because testing is built into term generation, but needs executable generators.
numbers: Rabe et al. skip-tree conjecturing: between 13% and 30% of generated statements were both provable and new, as reported in the survey.
limits: Secondhand figure here; checked against the primary in a10.
agent_relevance: A model proposer needs a cheap truth filter (test or counterexample search) before the costly prover. Without it most proposals are false, copies or trivial.

source: Johansson, Rosen, Smallbone and Claessen (2014) Hipster: Integrating Theory Exploration in a Proof Assistant
finding: Hipster runs QuickSpec inside Isabelle/HOL. Conjectures are tested on random values (default 200 tests, stop if classes stable over the last 100, else double). It drops any lemma that routine reasoning (no induction) proves. Proved lemmas are tagged and reused for later conjectures. It has an exploratory mode and a proof mode that looks for the lemma missing from the current goal.
numbers: Default 200 initial random tests; stops when no new lemma was proved since the last open-conjecture pass. Isabelle kernel checks every proof.
quote: Hipster discards all lemmas that can be proved by routine reasoning
limits: Demonstration paper, no benchmark rates in this text. Pass rate depends on the tactic called 'difficult reasoning'.
agent_relevance: Define 'routine' by what the base solver already does, and keep only lemmas beyond it. That is a concrete worth test for a stored lemma.

source: Nagashima, Xu, Wang, Goc and Bang (2022) Template-Based Conjecturing for Automated Induction in Isabelle/HOL (TBC)
finding: A fixed set of general templates (identity, commutativity, associativity and the like) instead of random term generation keeps the number of conjectures low. TBC proves or refutes the conjectures, then retries the original goal with proved ones as lemmas.
numbers: Largest gain 40 percentage points on the Prod problem set. IsaPlanner set: 60% solved without any conjecture, so little to gain. Weak on the hardest TIP15 set (327 problems, 15 min limit). Running example: 10 conjectures proved, only 2 used for the final goal; 8 of 10 unused.
quote: keeping the number of conjectures low is the main challenge in other conjecturing tools
limits: Baseline is an earlier induction prover (TAP21). Benchmarks are inductive proofs on functional programs. Time limits short for TIP15.
agent_relevance: Fixed templates of well-known properties beat open generation on cost. Expect most proved conjectures (here 8 of 10) not to be needed for the target. Value is in the few that are.

source: Rabe, Lee, Bansal and Szegedy (2020) Mathematical Reasoning via Self-supervised Skip-tree Training
finding: A language model trained to fill masked parts of HOL Light theorems can propose assumptions and equation sides. Proposals were checked by the DeepHOL prover and then by whether later proofs used them.
numbers: Provable / provable-and-new: assumptions task 32.19%/26.20% (uniform data), equalities 19.61%/12.28%, free-form conjecturing 82.32%/12.70% (uniform) and 97.75%/0.59% (weighted). Usefulness: 3445 of 3857 assumption theorems, 979 of 3440 equality theorems and 49 of 130 free-form theorems were used at least once in over 200,000 proofs each.
quote: there are simply many more ways to write a false statement than a true statement
limits: Prover proves only about 58% of validation theorems, so true rates are lower bounds. Use as premise survives a pruning step: a low bar. Trivial truths (predicting False, x = x) seen on inspection.
agent_relevance: The headline 13-30% 'new and true' is the realistic yield for model-proposed lemmas. Free-form output is mostly copies or trivial. Always ask whether a lemma was used in a pruned proof, not only whether it is true.

source: Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) Learning-assisted Theorem Proving with Millions of Lemmas
finding: Only a tiny fraction of lemmas in HOL Light and Flyspeck are named and reused. The authors mined the inference graph to score all intermediate lemmas for usefulness (dependency counts, size, PageRank, graph cutting, epcllemma) and added the best to the premise pool, with learned premise selection.
numbers: Core HOL Light, 1954 theorems: old best 14 methods 63.1%, union 65.4%. Fully honest evaluation: 61.7% to 64.8%, about a 5% relative gain; best single metric Q2 46.2% at 512 premises. Chained conjecturing (guessing mid-proof lemmas): Q2 54.5% rises to 61.4% (chain1) and 63.8% (chain 1-3), 12.6% and 17.0% relative. Flyspeck subset: 21.4% over older methods, but partly from other changes. Flyspeck has 1.95 billion inference edges and about 1.7 billion intermediate lemmas.
quote: only a tiny fraction of such statements is named and re-used in later proofs
limits: Gains in the cheating and almost-honest scenarios are inflated because a nearby lemma from the target's own proof is available. Honest gain is small (5%). Authors say a realistic Flyspeck gain is about 10%.
agent_relevance: Choosing which lemmas to keep matters, but honest gains from adding mined lemmas are modest (about 5%). Strict held-out scoring is needed (guardrail G3). Duplicates and alpha-variants must be merged.

source: Wang et al. (2024) LEGO-Prover: Neural Theorem Proving with Growing Libraries
finding: A prover and an evolver share a growing library of verified lemmas (skills) in vector stores. The prover splits an informal proof into steps, retrieves skills, and writes a modular formal proof. New lemmas from successful proofs are stored. The evolver generalises lemmas (directional transformation) and solves requests for missing lemmas, using miniF2F statements as hints.
numbers: ChatGPT, 100 attempts: miniF2F-valid 57.0% (prior best 52.4%), miniF2F-test 50.0% (prior 45.5%) in the ICLR version. Later arXiv v3 headline 50.4% valid / 47.1% test with human informal proofs. With model-written informal proofs 52.4% valid, 45.5% test. 257 of 488 problems solved.
limits: Numbers differ between paper versions (50.0% vs 47.1% on test). Isabelle. ChatGPT-class model. One run per setting, cost about 300 USD per 100-attempt run.
agent_relevance: Reusable verified lemmas from earlier attempts raise success by a few points in a loop with a retriever. Gains are modest but real.

source: Wang et al. (2024) LEGO-Prover: Neural Theorem Proving with Growing Libraries
finding: Ablation on miniF2F-valid with 50 attempts: removing the growing skill library (and the evolver) lowers the pass rate. The gap is small at first and widens as the library grows.
numbers: With library 50.4%, without 47.1% (3.3 points) at 50 attempts. Library reached 22,532 skills. Origin of skills: 10.8% from the prover, 38.2% from the evolver's request solver, 51.1% from the evolver's directional transformation. The authors admit some lemmas are trivially true or already in Isabelle's library.
quote: the advantage of adding the skill library is initially minimal
limits: Ablation only on valid set at 50 attempts. No count of how many of the 22,532 skills were ever retrieved or used. Generalised lemmas dominate the library.
agent_relevance: Library benefit is delayed and small (3.3 points). Skills need time to accumulate. No data on the useful fraction of 22.5k skills, so we must measure reuse ourselves.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025) Discovering New Theorems via LLMs with In-Context Proof Learning in Lean (Conjecturing-Proving Loop)
finding: CPL keeps conjecturing and proving as separate calls. A conjecturer (GPT-4o) writes statements given the library of proved theorems; a prover (o3) proves them with Lean feedback and up to 16 trials; verified pairs join the library, which is fed back as context. The baseline writes statement and proof in one call.
numbers: Topology notions (alpha-open sets). CPL: 30 loops, 269 theorems. Simple-loop baseline: 400 loops, 359 theorems, with shorter proofs and without the target results (e.g. alpha-open intersection, semi-open and preopen intersections).
quote: the simple loop framework tends to generate easily provable theorems
limits: One topic, one run each, no variance. Proof length used as the difficulty proxy. Different models in the two arms (GPT-4o and o3 vs o3 alone).
agent_relevance: Letting the same call both state and prove drifts to easy statements. Separate the proposer from the prover so the proposer is not rewarded for provability.

source: Kasaura et al. (2025) Discovering New Theorems via LLMs with In-Context Proof Learning in Lean (Conjecturing-Proving Loop)
finding: Putting the self-generated library in the prover's context improves proving, including a theorem it could not prove otherwise.
numbers: Re-proving the 269 generated theorems: 99% (267) with prior library as context, 90% (242) with definitions only. Target theorem alpha-open intersection, 128 tries each: proved only in the setting with the generated library. In natural language (16 tries) models mostly judged the true statement false. Theorem arrived after 49 generated theorems.
limits: Contexts for re-proving contain earlier lemmas that may be near-copies of the target, so some of the 9-point gain is lookup. Tiny sample for the target (one theorem).
agent_relevance: Prior proved lemmas in context act as worked examples and as stepping stones. The effect on proofs it could not otherwise make is the case for a lemma store.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
finding: One model plays conjecturer and prover. The conjecturer sees a seed theorem with proof plus a lemma used in it and writes a related conjecture. It is trained on conjectures that are barely provable by the current prover (pass rate in (0, 1/4]), after dropping ones with a low proof-length to statement-length ratio (the lowest 20%, an elegance filter) and re-weighting by Wasserstein distance to the unproved statements.
numbers: 51.3B tokens in Lean. LeanWorkbook proved 28.5% vs 13.2% for the best expert iteration. miniF2F-test 65.0% (pass@3200), ProofNet-test 23.9%, PutnamBench 8/644. Re-training with generated conjectures added 2-3 points on miniF2F and ProofNet at pass@128.
limits: Training method, not a scaffold. Compute is large. LeanWorkbook is partly unprovable: of 20 unproved statements, 7 were provable, so the best possible rate is 38.7%-68.5% (95% CI).
agent_relevance: The useful conjecture is one near the edge of what the prover can do, not one it always proves or never proves. A scaffold can log pass rate per proposed lemma and keep those in a middle band.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
finding: Why conjectures help: they give dense feedback where the real targets give almost none. On unproved dataset statements, sampling proofs mostly fails; generated conjectures near the edge succeed often enough to learn from.
numbers: At a checkpoint with 11.4% pass rate on LeanWorkbook, only 131 of 2.5M generated proofs of the 79K unproved statements were correct. At least 47% of generated conjectures were proved. Earlier work cited: 98.5% of sampling compute produced no proof.
limits: Pass-rate figures are from training runs of a fine-tuned model. Not shown to transfer to prompting.
agent_relevance: For hard targets, many attempts give no signal. Intermediate lemmas the agent can actually prove turn a flat failure into graded progress.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) Subgoal-based demonstration learning, and Jiang et al. (2022) Thor; cited in LEGO-Prover Table 1
finding: Baselines against which LEGO-Prover is compared on miniF2F: search-based Thor (with expert iteration) and ChatGPT-based Subgoal-Learning. LLM-based modular methods beat fine-tuned search methods in this table.
numbers: Thor 39.3% test, Thor + expert iteration 45.5% test (48.0% valid), Subgoal-Learning ChatGPT 45.5% test (52.4% valid), LEGO-Prover 50.0% test (57.0% valid), plain baselines 28.3% valid / 29.9% test.
limits: Rows read from the LEGO-Prover table; baselines not opened separately. Attempt counts differ across rows.
agent_relevance: Provides the control: modular proofs with retrieved lemmas beat flat proof generation at similar model size.

source: Lemmanaid, Alhessi et al. (2025), as cited in MathlibLemma
finding: Cited as a related system that targets lemma discovery with neural conjecturing plus symbolic filtering for Isabelle. Not read.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Only a citation seen in another paper.
agent_relevance: Candidate for the next pass (angle B). No claim taken from it.

source: MathlibLemma (2026) Folklore Lemma Generation and Benchmark for Formal Mathematics
finding: Four-stage pipeline (Discovery, Judge, Formalizer, Prover) mines folklore lemmas missing from Mathlib, seeded by one Mathlib file at a time. Splitting the stages separates failure modes: false math, syntax errors, proof failure. The Judge filters semantically false candidates before costly Lean work.
numbers: Funnel on 109 seed files (GPT-5.1): proposed 3427 / 2591 / 3130 (foundational / applied / abstract). Judge-accepted 71.4% / 66.6% / 63.2%. Compilable after repair 77.1% / 70.6% / 61.3%. Trivial 4.1% / 6.6% / 10.8%. Final benchmark 4,028 statements. Judge dropped 30-37% of raw candidates; audit of 53 rejected: 54% really false, 46% valid (false negatives).
limits: Generation model and judge are the same model family (GPT-5.1), so the set reflects its view. Seed-file local, one-shot discovery. No test that the statements are useful, only novel and non-trivial.
agent_relevance: Staged filters work, but the judge loses almost half valid items among those it rejects. Do not make the model judge the only gate.

source: MathlibLemma (2026) Folklore Lemma Generation and Benchmark for Formal Mathematics
finding: Proving the discovered lemmas is hard closed-book. Different provers solve different lemmas, so the union is far above any single model. An expert audit shows most unsolved items are provable.
numbers: Success@2 (one try plus two repairs): GPT-Reasoning 19.39%, Goedel 17.70%, GPT 15.69%, Kimina 10.70%, DeepSeek-32B 6.98%, DeepSeek-70B 6.68%, Qwen 2.46%. Union of all 37.39% (foundational 47.48%, applied 27.48%, abstract 30.93%). Goedel 27.42% foundational but 8.24% abstract. Expert audit: 107 of 138 residual (78%) provable, so solvable fraction near 86%.
limits: Closed-book, no Mathlib search. Success@2 is a small budget. Benchmark built by one pipeline.
agent_relevance: Proposing a lemma is easier than proving it. Different attempt types fail on different items, which supports varied operators over a fixed list but not persona voters on one answer (G4).

source: MathlibLemma (2026) Folklore Lemma Generation and Benchmark for Formal Mathematics
finding: External check of usefulness: a small pilot sent six cleaned lemmas to Mathlib. Pipeline cost is low per item.
numbers: Six submitted: three merged, one rejected as redundant with existing material, two not pursued. 1,506 released proofs after the proof-bypass screen (no sorry, axiom, constant, opaque). Cost about 200 USD for 4,028 statements (0.05 each), proving about 500 USD, 0.46 USD per proof all-in.
limits: Six items, hand-cleaned and curated, so 3 of 6 is not a rate for the pipeline. Maintainer review cost excluded.
agent_relevance: Only about half of curated generated lemmas passed expert review; one was a duplicate of existing material. Check for duplicates against the library before storing.

source: Fajtlowicz (1988) On conjectures of Graffiti; as described in Johansson and Smallbone (2021)
finding: Graffiti made graph theory conjectures of fixed shapes and tested them against a library of example graphs. Because the example set was fixed, it kept producing many non-theorems. Systems that generate fresh test data on demand avoid this.
numbers: No counts given in the survey.
limits: Primary Graffiti papers not read; claim is the survey's description.
agent_relevance: A conjecture filter is only as good as its test examples. Use a growing pool of counterexamples that new conjectures must pass, not a fixed set.

source: Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) Learning-assisted Theorem Proving with Millions of Lemmas
finding: Quality of a lemma is estimated from the proof graph: how many later statements depend on it (usefulness U), how much it saves (D), its size, and whether it is a conjunction of two others. Duplicates and alpha-variants must be merged first. Doubled size often means a mere conjunction.
numbers: Proof recording for Flyspeck took 29 hours CPU. About 33% of clauses from 200,000 core lemmas were subsumed. 2,076,682 partially de-duplicated core lemmas shrank to 1,076,995 after alpha-normalisation.
limits: Measured on human-made proofs, where the lemma is an intermediate step of a real proof. Not on newly conjectured lemmas.
agent_relevance: Cheap worth scores from the reuse graph: count dependents, penalise size and conjunctions, merge variants. This gives code-side selection (G5) with no model judgment.

source: Lenat and Brown (1983/1984) Why AM and Eurisko Appear to Work
finding: The paper argues that theory formation works on form, theories concern content, and discovery depends on a natural mapping between the two. A system that mutates structure can say nothing about meaning; minimal structural generalisations need not be minimal meaning generalisations.
numbers: No numeric result.
quote: we can only mutate the structural form of that concept
limits: Philosophical. Applies to symbol-edit style proposers.
agent_relevance: Ask for lemmas in the same representation the checker uses (statement text plus formal check). A proposal that cannot be checked cannot be graded.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
finding: Design details that guard against degenerate conjecturing: the conjecturer's reward cannot depend on each item alone or it collapses to one mode, so a Wasserstein re-weighting toward the real unproved targets keeps topics varied. An elegance filter discourages artificially hard conjectures with long goals.
numbers: Pass-rate band (0, 1/4]; remove lowest 20% by ratio of minimal proof length to conjecture length. Lemma-in-proof must be used in the conjecture's proof.
limits: Heuristics chosen by the authors. Ablations are summarised, not isolated for each filter in the text we read.
agent_relevance: Three checks for a stored lemma: it is near the edge of current ability, it is not bulky, and it covers the same topics as the open goals.

source: Nagashima et al. (2022) Template-Based Conjecturing (TBC); and Johansson and Smallbone (2021)
finding: Two schools of conjecturing for induction: top-down (lemmas made from the stuck proof attempt) and bottom-up (lemmas made from available functions and datatypes to enrich the background theory). HipSpec and Hipster generate randomly in the bottom-up style; TBC uses templates; RoughSpec uses equation templates for Haskell.
numbers: No numbers beyond a09.
limits: Classification by the TBC authors.
agent_relevance: Our schema can use both: bottom-up lemma store, top-down 'what lemma would unstick this step' as a repair operator triggered by a failed check (G1, G2).

source: Johansson and Smallbone (2021) overview and Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) combined reading
finding: Across systems, the yield pattern is the same: many candidates, a small fraction true, a smaller fraction new, a still smaller fraction used. Examples: skip-tree 12-26% new and true; LEGO-Prover 22.5k skills for a 3-point ablation gain; TBC 2 of 10 proved lemmas used; HOL Light honest gain about 5%.
numbers: See a09, a10, a11, a13. Used fraction among proved lemmas: 2 of 10 (TBC example); 28% (979 of 3440) for equalities and 89% (3445 of 3857) for assumptions in a10.
limits: Synthesis across different systems and different definitions of use. Not a pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: Plan for a low useful fraction. Store lemmas with a use counter, retire ones never retrieved, and report reuse rate as a measured quantity.
